item.title: Is AI becoming a new religion?
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Why AI resembles a charismatic religious leader • Why a decade of AI safety promises keep failing to bite • Trump wants an AI Force like Space Force, but that could make AI’s risks harder to manage • Why most health apps are biased even before their first lines of code are written • We’ve tracked $80M of spending on almost 170 AI-generated political ads this year – it’s weird
item.content:encoded:
What happens when a person moves from asking a chatbot for emotional support and advice to spiritual guidance? AI is already transforming the practice of religion in many ways, but a scholar of religion delves into whether AI represents a new kind of religious movement. Also this week, a couple of articles examine the daunting challenges regulating AI technology at an international level, another piece examines the bias inherent in AI-infused health monitoring apps, and a look at the varied – and sometimes odd – ways AI is shaking up political campaigns in the U.S.

Lead Story

Why AI resembles a charismatic religious leader

Morgan Shipley, Michigan State University

AI can function as a charismatic figure without standing on a stage, establishing a church or gathering disciples, writes a scholar of religion.

At this point, AI clearly offers something more significant than access to information. By helping people interpret their lives, AI is entering territory historically occupied by therapists, spiritual advisers and religious communities.

Regulation

Why a decade of AI safety promises keep failing to bite

Jon Whittle, The University of Melbourne

Donald Trump’s White House Accord on Super Intelligence looks set to join a long line of ineffectual calls for self-regulation from the tech industry.

Trump wants an AI Force like Space Force, but that could make AI’s risks harder to manage

Jason M. Blazakis, Middlebury College

An AI Force would likely push China to create its own. That arms race could turn a technology already slipping out of human control into a weapon.

Health

Why most health apps are biased even before their first lines of code are written

Mahima Kalla, The University of Melbourne; Noushin Nazarian, The University of Melbourne

Apps and wearables are often built on invisible assumptions that might not be relevant to you. A new study shows how we can change that.

Politics

We’ve tracked $80M of spending on almost 170 AI-generated political ads this year – it’s weird

Travis N. Ridout, Washington State University; Erika Franklin Fowler, Wesleyan University; Michael Franz, Bowdoin College

Almost 170 ads and $80 million in spending and only 31% with a disclaimer: Here’s what researchers found when they tracked AI in this year’s campaign ads.

item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • I’m a physicist who worked on the Nobel-winning neutrino search – here’s how a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice became a telescope for ghost particles from space • Nobel laureate Karl Deisseroth on how light is changing what we know about the brain • Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules • French student protests: comparisons with 1968 will only serve the political extremes • Is this the ‘mathocalypse’? Why OpenAI’s latest results dump has left mathematicians in shock • Coolcations: tourism boom is taking a toll on chillier destinations
item.content:encoded:
When Karl Deisseroth was studying to be a doctor in the 1990s, he took a rotation working with psychiatric patients.

It ​s​tarted him down a path of discovery about how the brain works that would eventually lead him to become a Nobel laureate.​ “The brain is billions of fragile, extremely vulnerable, transparent, very fast-acting cells,” Deisseroth said in an interview for The Conversation Weekly podcast.

“I was impressed by the magnitude of the challenge.” He reflects on how his research pioneered the field of optogenetics, a new tool that uses light to control nerve cells to investigate how their activity shapes our feelings and behaviour​.

Other scientific endeavours rewarded by the Nobel committees this week include a giant observatory at the South Pole, built to capture glimpses of neutrinos, ghostly messengers from space. A scientist who worked on the project explains what it’s like to work there. And we explain the science behind the mirror-image molecules that won the Nobel prize in chemistry.

And as Canadian poet Anne Carson was named the new Nobel laureate for literature, a classics expert appreciates how she discovered new possibilities within language.

Gemma Ware

Head of Audio, The Conversation UK

item.title: Why an obscure US accounting proposal is causing an outcry
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • US regulators want to make corporate earnings reports less frequent, but investors have doubts • An iced coffee won’t predict job performance — but it might reveal hiring bias • Global health research makes America richer and healthier • Criminal conspiracy to steal used cooking oil shows how trash can become treasure • Hunter-gatherer societies are often put on a pedestal as paragons of equality – but the reality is more complicated • Does increased childcare funding help mothers into work?
item.content:encoded:
What would investors and markets do if they had less timely information on a company’s financial health?

The U.S. may find out soon. One of its top financial regulators, the Securities and Exchange Commission, is considering a rule that would let public companies report earnings only every six months as opposed to every three, which has been the case for decades. While this proposal may sound obscure, it has sparked opposition that has shattered records in terms of public comments filed. Many of them are from ordinary investors and retirement savers.

Tzachi Zach, a scholar of accounting at The Ohio State University, constructed a tracker using artificial intelligence to gauge the sentiment of these comments. The top concern, he found, is that “less frequent reporting would make it harder for investors to monitor companies’ performance and decision-making, because key information is withheld for longer periods.”

There are other risks as well, he notes, especially when it comes to companies raising capital.

Helen Fessenden

Senior Economy and Business Editor, The Conversation U.S.

US regulators want to make corporate earnings reports less frequent, but investors have doubts

Tzachi Zach, The Ohio State University

    Longzhou Wang, University of Alberta

    Patrick Parenteau, Vermont Law & Graduate School

item.title: How Nobel scientists learned to control brain cells with light
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • How pond algae led to a Nobel prize and a new way to study the brain • Optogenetics wins the Nobel – one neuroscience breakthrough in a line of technological innovations helping scientists map and control the brain • Brazil elections 2026: First-round victories demand a commitment to democracy by the far-right that has not yet been made
item.content:encoded:
How do you switch on a brain cell with a beam of light?

Three scientists who worked out the answer have won this year’s Nobel prize in physiology or medicine. Hailing their work, Robert Lucas, a professor of neuroscience at the University of Manchester, explains how a protein found in a tiny alga led to optogenetics, a technique that is changing how we study the brain. It is also being tested in people with a form of sight loss.

For her part, Kimberlee D'Ardenne revisits some of the technological advances that have supported the current understanding of how the brain works. And that can point to where neuroscience might be going next.

Brazilians have to wait until October 25 for clarity on who will serve as their next president. Right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro beat left-wing President Lula da Silva in the first round of polling but failed to win an outright majority. Hence a runoff later this month. Débora Thomé writes that, whoever emerges the winner, the rule remains the same: the election must be fair, and the loser must accept the result. The future of democracy in the country depends on it.

Clint Witchalls

Senior Health Editor

How pond algae led to a Nobel prize and a new way to study the brain

Robert Lucas, University of Manchester

Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won for optogenetics, a technique that uses light to switch brain cells on and off.

Optogenetics wins the Nobel – one neuroscience breakthrough in a line of technological innovations helping scientists map and control the brain

Kimberlee D'Ardenne, Arizona State University

Neuroscientific advances follow a pattern of visualizing the brain, measuring its function and then controlling it. Optogenetics may lead to a new era of medical treatment.

    Patrick Ngassa Piotie, University of Pretoria

    John Mukum Mbaku, Weber State University

    Monideepa Tarafdar, UMass Amherst

    Prompting AI models to contradict your ideas can improve your thinking about a problem.

item.title: Unregulated AI and security threats
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Trump frames unregulated AI as a way to keep ahead of China – but in fact, it harms US national security • US tech leaders are urgently calling for rules on AI – China already has them • Meta wants people to use ‘AI agents’ to do daily tasks for them. Here’s why that’s a problem • The ‘War Games’ problem: Computer science has long understood what it takes to keep AI under control • Using an AI chatbot to practice new languages can be helpful, but it doesn’t replace speaking with an actual person
item.content:encoded:
When we started this newsletter on artificial intelligence, we very deliberately decided that it would not be only about technology, because the story of AI in society is so broad. The discussion around whether and how to regulate AI reflects that complexity. In one piece this week, an international relations scholar argues that the Trump administration’s opposition to regulation – under the argument that there’s a global race that regulation would slow – actually benefits Chinese companies. And a cybersecurity researcher reveals that China has been regulating algorithms and AI usage for years. Elsewhere this week, an ethics expert makes the case that blaming AIs for “rogue” actions can be misguided, and a critical look at Meta’s new Muse AI agent technology.

Lead Story

Trump frames unregulated AI as a way to keep ahead of China – but in fact, it harms US national security

Stephen Collins, Kennesaw State University

An unregulated sector has risks in itself but will also aid the rapid advancement of AI in China.

China uses a process known as distillation to exploit cutting-edge U.S. AI models to train China's own models. The process enables China to develop models nearly as powerful but much more efficient, using far fewer resources... As a result of its distillation strategy, the pace of China's AI progress is tightly linked to U.S. progress.

Regulation

US tech leaders are urgently calling for rules on AI – China already has them

Madeline Carr, UCL

China has already implemented many rules governing the use of artificial intelligence.

Agents

Meta wants people to use ‘AI agents’ to do daily tasks for them. Here’s why that’s a problem

Francesco Bailo, University of Sydney; Rob Nicholls, University of Sydney

Meta can’t beat its rivals on raw AI capability. With its new Muse agent, it doesn’t need to.

Technology

The ‘War Games’ problem: Computer science has long understood what it takes to keep AI under control

Deven Desai, Georgia Institute of Technology

A hit 1983 movie illustrates what computer scientists have long known: If you give an AI agent a goal but don’t control what it can and can’t do, you shouldn’t be surprised by what it does.

Using an AI chatbot to practice new languages can be helpful, but it doesn’t replace speaking with an actual person

Antonio Perez-Nunez, College of Charleston

People might feel more comfortable making mistakes if they’re interacting with AI chatbots. But they will miss the nuances that come from conversing with real people.

item.title: FlyDubai and the Israeli election
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Flydubai attack feeds into Netanyahu’s ‘protector’ narrative with crucial elections approaching • Could a former IDF chief break Benjamin Netanyahu’s grip on power in Israel? • With a tragedy averted, the Flydubai incident has put cockpit security under new scrutiny • Almost everyone naturally turns left when walking – and we still have no idea why • The ‘War Games’ problem: Computer science has long understood what it takes to keep AI under control • Manchester City supporters have been gaslit. What happens now?
item.content:encoded:
The attempted hijacking of FlyDubai flight FZ1073 has put a few people in focus, not least the wounded pilot who managed to open the cockpit door and the passengers who rushed in to help subdue the co-pilot.

But back in Israel, it is how the the near-tragedy might affect the fortunes of Benjamin Netanyahu that is stimulating some of the coverage.

The motive of the co-pilot – seemingly bent on crashing the airplane and killing the mainly Israeli passengers – has not been publicly established. But with crucial elections just weeks away, the Israeli prime minister can already point to the event to further his narrative of a country under attack and in need of his firm guidance.

As Middle East expert Ran Porat notes: “Netanyahu was quick to incorporate the plane attack into his campaign by posting on his social media accounts a video and images of him embracing and praising one of the passengers (a Netanyahu supporter) who stormed the cockpit, his shirt still stained with blood.”

But will it be enough to save him in the upcoming vote. Speaking prior to the FlyDubai incident, Israeli politics scholar Dov Waxman sat down with The Conversation Weekly podcast to explain what is at stake in the election and assess Netanyahu’s chances of defying the polls and a strong challenge from Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of the Israel Defense Forces and leader of the newly formed Yashar party.

Elsewhere this week, we have been monitoring the escalating fighting in Ethiopia and pondering: why do people tend to turn left when walking?

Matt Williams

Senior International Editor

Top story

Israeli passengers arrive back in Israel after the attempted hijacking of a passenger plane over Saudi Arabia. Abir Sultan/EPA

Ran Porat, Monash University

Could a former IDF chief break Benjamin Netanyahu’s grip on power in Israel?

Isabella Podwinski, The Conversation; Justin Bergman, The Conversation

With a tragedy averted, the Flydubai incident has put cockpit security under new scrutiny

Steven Leib, CQUniversity Australia; Guido Carim Junior, CQUniversity Australia

Iñaki Echeverría Huarte, Universidad de Navarra; Ángel Garcimartín Montero, Universidad de Navarra; Iker Zuriguel Ballaz, Universidad de Navarra

Across ages, genders, cultures and conditions, crowds always walk in a counter-clockwise spiral.

The ‘War Games’ problem: Computer science has long understood what it takes to keep AI under control

Deven Desai, Georgia Institute of Technology

A hit 1983 movie illustrates what computer scientists have long known: If you give an AI agent a goal but don’t control what it can and can’t do, you shouldn’t be surprised by what it does.

Manchester City supporters have been gaslit. What happens now?

Josh Bland, University of Cambridge

The evidence now requires Manchester City supporters to make the distinction their owners have spent years blurring.

    Julian Koplin, Monash University; The University of Melbourne

    Lethal injections are not typically administered by doctors, given executions are incompatible with their oath to protect lives.

  • One in three Ukrainian civilians estimated to meet the criteria for PTSD or complex PTSD – new study

    Gwendolyn Sasse, Centre for East European and International Studies (ZOiS); University of Oxford; Deirdre MacManus, King's College London

    War-related trauma now affects most people in Ukraine and presents a major threat to the country’s resiliance in the face of continuing Russian aggression.

    Catherine A. Sanderson, Amherst College

    Alemayehu Fentaw Weldemariam, Indiana University

    An offensive in the Tigray region followed months of aerial strikes by the Ethiopian government. The situation could spark a wider regional conflict.

    Ivor Chipkin, University of Pretoria

    Sara Harmouch, George Washington University

    More women are taking up training and recruiting positions in the Islamic State group and other militant organizations.

item.title: Shocked at price of filling your car? It could get worse
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Why fuel prices may go higher still • AI has made borrowing more expensive – an expert explains how bond markets are changing • Gen Z communicates differently in the workplace, but older colleagues can still decode them • Cities keep shelling out taxpayer money for sports stadiums, yet the economics almost never makes sense • How Trump’s crypto winnings undermined the industry’s push for looser regulation • How smoking makes Australians poorer – and what we can do about it
item.content:encoded:
When the Strait of Hormuz shut in early March, after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, petroleum industry analysts projected crude oil prices could reach $150 or even $200 a barrel.

Seven months later, they’ve only just topped $100, thanks to various efforts to keep oil prices from skyrocketing, write Joshua Busby and Greg Pollock, U.S.-based scholars of the energy industry and national security.

But the cushions that have forestalled the nightmare scenarios so far have run their course, Busby and Pollock write. And as the war continues, the strait is still shut. They explain why “significant price hikes – and perhaps even shortages – may be on the way."t

Jeff Inglis

Environment + Energy Editor, The Conversation US

Why fuel prices may go higher still

Joshua Busby, The University of Texas at Austin; Greg Pollock, Georgetown University

Seven months into the US conflict with Iran, with no clear end in sight, the global oil market has now largely exhausted the safety measures that exist to keep a lid on petroleum prices.

—

    Akhil Bhardwaj, University of Bath

item.title: El Niño's deadly heat threat to the Sahel
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Nigeria faces the world’s highest projected death toll from super El Niño heat: what could save lives • Yemen’s Houthis move to control crucial waterway – our research maps the countries most at risk
item.content:encoded:
Nigeria, Sudan, Niger and Chad face tens of thousands of additional deaths over the coming months as the super El Niño brings extreme heat to countries where many people cannot afford to keep cool. Michael Greenstone, Tamma Carleton, Genevieve Maricle and Emily Grover-Kopec explain why the risks are so high and how governments can act now to save lives by issuing heat warnings, providing drinking water and places to cool down, and protecting outdoor workers.

There’s another battle for control raging over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a maritime chokepoint between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Academics have mapped which countries would be most affected by a Houthi blockade.

Anna Weekes

Environment + Energy Editor, Africa

Nigeria faces the world’s highest projected death toll from super El Niño heat: what could save lives

Michael Greenstone, University of Chicago; Tamma Carleton, University of California, Berkeley

The super El Niño could cause 31,400 extra heat deaths in Nigeria alone. Heat warnings, cooling centres and worker protections could help save lives.

Yemen’s Houthis move to control crucial waterway – our research maps the countries most at risk

Johannes Lumma, University of Oxford; Jasper Verschuur, Delft University of Technology

  • Why fuel prices may go higher still

item.title: Could AI really wipe out humanity? 5 scenarios
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • How would AI actually kill all humans? Here are the top 5 scenarios • AI can be more comforting than a person – our research shows why • Russia-Ukraine war is accelerating the dangerous race toward fully autonomous drones • Why AI has trouble predicting the fury of hurricane intensity • Government hacks, rogue agents and no transparency: can we ever fully trust AI?
item.content:encoded:
When ChatGPT first launched publicly, the mood among consumers seemed to be mostly amazement. Four years later, the narrative around the future of artificial intelligence has become decidedly dark. This week’s newsletter reflects that dramatic shift with a story on the most likely scenarios of AI systems getting outside human control and a podcast discussing what regulations might look like. We also look at the advancement of autonomous drones in the Ukraine-Russia war and why chatbots can appear more comforting than human companions.

Lead Story

How would AI actually kill all humans? Here are the top 5 scenarios

Toby Walsh, UNSW

The most probable scenario is likely not what you think.

Imagine – and it doesn’t take a lot of imagination – that AI causes massive job losses, pollutes the information space with misinformation, fractures our politics, and destroys human relationships with fake synthetic companionship.

Society might easily break. Slowly but surely, we’d stop being able to support human life at any scale.

AI and Humanity

AI can be more comforting than a person – our research shows why

Sarah A. Walker, Durham University; Belen Lopez-Perez, University of Manchester

We increasingly turn to chatbots when we are upset. But what they cannot do may be what matters most.

Military

Russia-Ukraine war is accelerating the dangerous race toward fully autonomous drones

Amy McAuliffe, University of Notre Dame

Drones with autonomous functions reduce dependence on communications links and can escape attempts at jamming. But they come with huge ethical risks.

Technology

Why AI has trouble predicting the fury of hurricane intensity

Chanh Kieu, Indiana University

Storms like 2026’s Hurricane Polo that rapidly intensify can catch communities off guard and leave little time to prepare or evacuate. Being able to forecast those risks can save lives.

Podcast 🎙️

Government hacks, rogue agents and no transparency: can we ever fully trust AI?

Gemma Ware, The Conversation

AI expert Nick Jennings speaks to The Conversation Weekly podcast about calls for a slowdown in the development of frontier AI models.

item.content:encoded:
As more incidents emerge of AI agents going rogue during testing, can we ​ever fully trust them? In the latest hack, Australia revealed OpenAI agents hacked into a government database containing health data – and took nearly three months to disclose the breach.

On the latest episode of The Conversation Weekly podcast, AI expert Nick Jennings says tech company leaders have choices about how they develop their models. “It’s not that they have to keep going ​… or that the AI is forcing them to keep going on and keep improving.​”

Experts remain sceptical about the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity, but calls for regulation are growing and dominated coverage of the White House summit between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump.

Jennings, who has researched multi-agentic AI for decades, says that while calls for a kill switch won’t be as simple as adding a “big red button” that turns the AI off, it’s important to have external control over the system.

Elsewhere this week we have been keeping an eye on goings-on at the United Nations and previewing the upcoming elections in Brazil.

item.content:encoded:
The arguments over remote and hybrid work aren’t going away more than six years after the COVID-19 pandemic started.

But what if this debate fixated less on, say, the CEO’s management style or specific workplace format and focused more closely on organizational culture? After all, this ranges from highly collaborative to extremely hierarchical, with many variations along the gamut.

Sebastian Fixson of Babson College believes culture is a powerful determinant in whether remote and hybrid policies work. He and his colleagues Gina O’Connor and Jonathan Sims looked at four global companies that took different routes during and after the pandemic as they tried to return operations to normal.

It was organizational culture, they found, that established how quickly an employer successfully established a balance between remote, on-site and hybrid work after the pandemic’s earliest phase.

“The hierarchical companies moved faster but struggled more with managerial issues over workplace policies,” he writes. “In contrast, the collaborative companies took longer to decide on their workplace policies but encountered less pushback from their employees.”

Senior Economy and Business Editor, The Conversation US

item.title: Trump and Xi: the touchy subjects on summit agenda
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Three Ts will dominate Trump-Xi summit – but expect little movement on trade, less on Taiwan and who knows on tech • Trump declares victory in Greenland, but the deal exposes a deeper crisis of trust
item.content:encoded:
It’s four months since Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump had their last summit. When they meet again on Thursday the odds are that they will focus on trade, technology and Taiwan.

But will they be able to come to any sort of transformative agreement on any? Rana Mitter has his doubts given the difficulties underlying each of the issues as well as the fact that the leaders seem to have fundamentally incompatible agendas on all three topics.

After months of demanding the United States take “total control” over Greenland, Trump announced he had struck a deal with the governments of Greenland and Denmark. He declared the new security deal a personal triumph, but, as Shannon Brincat and Juan Cáceres write, Denmark and Greenland confirmed the deal in more subdued terms.

On the face of it, it seems like everyone wins: Trump gets to declare victory, Denmark and Greenland get to keep nominal sovereignty, and NATO avoids a rupture. But there is a more troubling reading, too – and it rings alarm bells for democracy.

Caroline Southey

Founding Editor, Africa

item.title: Why AI labs push ahead despite doomsday talk
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • ‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans’: if AI labs are so worried about AI doom, why don’t they stop? • Russian team ‘misused’ Claude AI to train a killer drone on scraped Ukrainian war footage • No, AI systems don’t have a drive to survive – a developmental psychologist explains why it only looks that way • How AI could make us work even harder
item.content:encoded:
Experts have been warning for years that artificial intelligence could pose an existential threat to humanity, but this week marked a turning point, with even the CEOs of AI labs calling for a slowdown. What would that look like, and could nuclear proliferation pacts offer a model for regulating AI? Our experts offer analyses from different perspectives.

Lead Story

‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans’: if AI labs are so worried about AI doom, why don’t they stop?

Michael Noetel, The University of Queensland

A powerful mix of hopes, fears and arms-race dynamics means AI companies won’t slow down unless they’re forced to.

  • Is the nuclear non-proliferation pact a model for regulating runaway AI?

  • Tech leaders are calling for an ‘AI slowdown’ – but what would that mean in practice?

  • The decades-old ‘AI alignment problem’ has finally become a reality. Solving it won’t be easy

AI firms already report signs of 'recursive self-improvement,' where each model helps to build a better successor. According to OpenAI’s chief scientist, models are improving faster than humans’ ability to control them.

Military

In tests, some AI systems resisted being shut down. But an instinct to stay “alive” isn’t the reason they behaved that way.

How AI could make us work even harder
